title: SpaceX Wins FCC Nod for 15,000-Satellite VLEO Network as EU Confronts Its Empty Chip Tool Market
subhead: The FCC cleared a 15,000-satellite very-low-orbit direct-to-device constellation for SpaceX, extending Starlink into standard smartphones, while EU ministers debated a second Chips Act amid data showing ASML sold nothing in Europe this year.

sections.heading: SpaceX Cleared for 15,000-Satellite Direct-to-Device Layer
sections.body:
The FCC granted SpaceX regulatory approval on October 7 to launch and operate a 15,000-satellite Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) constellation dedicated to direct-to-device (D2D) satellite-to-cellular service, according to SatNews. The satellites will operate at altitudes between 326 and 335 kilometers — well below Starlink's main shells near 550 km — a design choice that reduces path loss and latency enough to link space-based payloads directly to standard, unmodified smartphones without special chips or directional antennas.

The authorization resolves a review the FCC opened in late 2025 and builds on earlier commission decisions covering spectrum-sharing and D2D frameworks, including SpaceX's $17 billion acquisition of 65 MHz of AWS-4 and H-Block mid-band spectrum from EchoStar. SatNews notes the VLEO band imposes continuous atmospheric drag, forcing electric-propulsion station-keeping and a permanent satellite-replacement pipeline.
sections.whyItMatters: Direct-to-device from orbit removes the terrestrial tower as the gatekeeper of mobile coverage. A 15,000-unit layer turns satellite-to-phone from a niche emergency service into a mass-market carrier function — and concentrates that capability in a single operator's hands.

sections.heading: EU Debates Chips Act 2.0 as ASML Reports Zero European Sales
sections.body:
EU industry ministers met in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the proposed European Chips Act 2.0, presented by the Commission on June 3 as part of a technological-sovereignty package, according to EU Today. The shift moves beyond subsidising production toward creating demand, securing supply chains, and hardening the bloc against disruption, alongside briefings on Critical Raw Materials Act strategic projects. The original Chips Act entered force in 2023 after shortages hit car and medical-equipment makers.

That debate landed against an awkward data point: ASML, Europe's largest chip-equipment maker, recorded a zero-percent revenue share in Europe in 2026, with an executive quoted saying the company has sold 'absolutely nothing' in the region this year (DatacenterDynamics, TechTimes). The company's sales are concentrated in Taiwan, South Korea, China, and the US.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap exposes a supply-side-only strategy: Europe builds fabs and tool subsidies but has almost no domestic demand for cutting-edge manufacturing. Chips Act 2.0's demand focus is a direct admission that production capacity without customers does not create sovereignty.

sections.heading: TSMC Weighs a Texas Hub That Could Top $265B
sections.body:
TSMC is reportedly considering a second US manufacturing hub, potentially in Dallas, that could include as many as six advanced wafer fabs and exceed the $265 billion committed to its Arizona complex, according to Taiwan's Economic Daily News via TrendForce. The report cites customer demand from Nvidia, Intel, AMD, and Apple and renewed Trump-administration threats of tariffs up to 200% on chipmakers that do not build in the US. TSMC had not commented on the report.

The move follows the existing Phoenix plan of six fabs, two advanced-packaging facilities, and an R&D center. TrendForce also reported that VIS and NXP are mulling a second Singapore fab as AI-driven foundry demand reshapes capacity plans.
sections.whyItMatters: Advanced-node capacity is being pulled out of Taiwan by tariff pressure and customer demand simultaneously. Each new US hub reduces the geographic concentration risk that has made Taiwan the single most contested node in the supply chain.

sections.heading: Malaysia's 'Silicon Island' Bets on Moving Up the Chip Value Chain
sections.body:
Malaysia is reclaiming a 2,300-acre man-made island south of Penang — dubbed Silicon Island — to expand its semiconductor footprint, Bloomberg reported via Yahoo. The project is expected to add a cumulative 1.1 trillion ringgit ($269 billion) to economic output through 2050 and create some 220,000 jobs by 2050. Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said space for growth around the existing Bayan Lepas cluster is 'increasingly constrained.'

Intel, AMD, and ASE Technology already operate around Bayan Lepas. Silicon Island is framed as a push beyond Malaysia's traditional assembly-and-test role into design and advanced packaging, riding AI demand for diversified production.
sections.whyItMatters: Southeast Asia is moving from back-end assembly toward higher-value packaging — exactly the segment where advanced AI chips are won or lost. Malaysia is positioning to capture value that currently flows almost entirely to Taiwan and South Korea.

sections.heading: Nvidia's $100B Ecosystem Bet Tied to Customer Concentration
sections.body:
Nvidia has completed more than $140 billion in transactions in a matter of months, with its equity portfolio approaching $100 billion in market value, as it shifts from pure chip sales toward a diversified AI ecosystem, per BigGo. The driver is customer concentration: three customers account for 44% of sales. Nvidia acquired open-source model platform Hugging Face for $12.9 billion and is in talks to invest about $1 billion in humanoid-robotics firm Figure, while participating in rounds for Perplexity and OpenAI.

In the SB Energy data-center project, Nvidia initially discussed up to $250 billion in credit support but compressed the first-phase guarantee to $105 billion after credit-default-swap spreads widened.
sections.whyItMatters: Nvidia is buying demand and building a moat beyond hardware because its revenue rests on a handful of hyperscalers. The credit-support pullback on SB Energy shows even the AI buildout's biggest beneficiary is now pricing in financing risk.

sections.heading: US-Australia Rare-Earth Pact Targets China's Refining Edge
sections.body:
President Trump and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a critical-minerals agreement at the White House described as an $8.5 billion deal, according to Asahi Shimbun. The pact targets Australia's rare-earth resources as Beijing tightens export rules. Earlier in the month, China announced it will require foreign companies to obtain government approval to export magnets containing even trace amounts of rare-earth material originating from China or produced with Chinese technology.

Separately, Greenland Mines said a US pact could strengthen mineral supply, and the Tanbreez rare-earths project in Greenland is advancing (Mining.com, Canadian Mining Journal).
sections.whyItMatters: The contest is not over who holds rare-earth ore but who controls refining and magnet production — the step China dominates. An $8.5 billion pact plus magnet-export approvals shows both sides are weaponising the processing stage, not the mine.

sections.heading: North Korea's Crypto Heists Fund the State — and Lead 2026
sections.body: North Korean hackers are suspected of stealing more than $351 million from crypto exchange Bitget in September — the largest known crypto heist of 2026, TechCrunch reported. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said the breach was 'highly consistent with known patterns of North Korean hacker organizations,' and the exchange pointed to a $464 million user-protection fund to cover losses. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributes the majority of 2026 crypto-hack value to North Korea. Reporting also flags the 'WaterPlum' group using deepfaked job interviews to target crypto developers (VOA, ABC).
sections.whyItMatters: State-directed crypto theft remains a core revenue channel for Pyongyang. The shift toward social-engineering and deepfake-driven infiltration — rather than pure exploits — makes attribution and defence harder for exchanges and developers.

sections.heading: South Korea's Nuri Rocket Hits Fourth Straight Success
sections.body:
South Korea's Nuri rocket delivered five primary satellites into orbit on October 7 — its fourth consecutive success and first five-satellite sequential deployment — with nine of ten secondary CubeSats also separating, according to The Star/AP. Korea AeroSpace Administration chief Oh Tae-seog said the mission demonstrated Nuri can deliver payloads 'to the orbit and at the time requested by customers.' It was the first of the programme's five launches to proceed without delay.

The capability tested — releasing multiple satellites accurately enough to keep them safely apart — is the same one needed for constellation deployment. Turkey's Anadolu Agency also covered the launch.
sections.whyItMatters: Multi-payload precision launch is the enabling skill for national satellite constellations. South Korea is converting a domestic launch vehicle into a commercial service, reducing its reliance on foreign rockets for its own space-based assets.

bottomLine: The day's clearest moves came from orbit and from Brussels. The FCC's approval of a 15,000-satellite SpaceX VLEO layer turns satellite-to-phone into a mass-market carrier function controlled by one operator; South Korea's Nuri hit its fourth straight success with a multi-payload mission, building the launch skill needed for national constellations. On the ground, EU ministers debated Chips Act 2.0 while ASML reported zero European tool sales — a stark gap between production subsidies and domestic demand. TSMC's potential Texas hub and Malaysia's Silicon Island both point to the same trend: advanced chipmaking capacity is being pulled out of Taiwan and pushed into the US and Southeast Asia. Nvidia's $100 billion ecosystem bet and its trimmed SB Energy credit guarantee showed the AI buildout's biggest winner hedging against revenue concentration, while the US-Australia rare-earth pact and North Korea's $351 million crypto heist confirmed that control of refining and of capital flows remains the real battleground.
sources: SatNews, EU Today, DatacenterDynamics, TechTimes, TrendForce, Economic Daily News, Bloomberg via Yahoo News SG, BigGo Finance, TechCrunch, TRM Labs, Asahi Shimbun, Mining.com, Canadian Mining Journal, The Star (AP), Anadolu Agency, VOA News, ABC News
